summary: RTP is used in many application areas and environments, which require different security mechanisms for confidentiality, integrity, and source authentication of RTP and RTCP packets. This informational document describes the available options.

plainLanguage.summary: Calls and videos can be protected in different ways depending on where they run. This lists the choices.

questions: what is the difference between dtls-srtp and sdes
subtitle: A guide to the many ways to protect RTP media, from SRTP and its key exchanges to DTLS, IPsec and DRM.

tldr.problem: RTP is used in very different settings, so no single mechanism can secure it, and developers struggle to choose among many solutions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys RTP topologies, the available mechanisms (SRTP with several key management options, IPsec, TLS, DTLS, content protection) and the requirements to weigh when choosing.
tldr.outcome: It gives guidance and examples but no normative recommendations. It reports that SRTP is widely deployed and that DTLS-SRTP is mandatory in WebRTC.

today: RFC 7201 is an Informational RFC that the metadata shows as neither obsoleted nor updated. It reflects the options at its April 2014 publication and, as it says, cannot be a complete survey since new mechanisms appear regularly.

sections.title: Why No Single Answer, and Session Topologies
sections.content:
RTP carries VoIP, conferencing, sensor data and IPTV, from point-to-point calls to large television distribution. This heterogeneity has prevented a single security solution, so many have been developed, and it is hard for developers to know what exists. The RFC gives an overview, guidance and an indication of actual and intended usage. It is not exhaustive and gives no normative recommendations.

A single mandated solution is not possible, but common mechanisms should be shared by related applications in common environments.

How RTP is arranged changes what security means.

  • Point-to-point: needs confidentiality, integrity and source authentication to stop third parties and man-in-the-middle attacks.
  • RTP mixer: creates a new stream with its own source identifier, so it must be trusted and holds the security context.
  • RTP translators: a transport translator may work without the security context, but a gateway often needs trust, and a media transcoder alters media and must be trusted.
  • Any Source Multicast: everyone with the group context can decrypt and verify, so a group context cannot separate individual sources.
  • Source-Specific Multicast: injecting traffic is harder but not impossible, and each role (media source, distribution source, feedback target, receiver) needs its own trust.
sections.plainLanguage: Different uses need different locks, so there is no one lock for everything. This guide shows the choices. A chat between two friends is easy to lock. A big group chat with helpers in the middle needs more care, because everyone with the key can read everything.

sections.title: Secure RTP and Its Transforms
sections.content:
SRTP provides confidentiality, integrity, source authentication and replay protection. It does not encrypt the RTP header or the first 8 bytes of the first RTCP packet header in each compound packet, which keeps header compression and third-party monitoring working, but the whole packet is integrity protected. The default transform is AES Counter Mode with 128-bit keys and HMAC-SHA-1 with an 80-bit authentication tag. Others listed include AES-f8, SEED, ARIA, AES-192-CM and AES-256-CM, AES-GCM and AES-CCM, and a NULL cipher.

Source authentication strength depends on the transform and key management; TESLA can give per-source authentication in some group cases but requires buffering. SRTP has no built-in key management and relies on an external protocol. The RFC says SRTP is widely deployed and the default transform is the most commonly used.
sections.plainLanguage: SRTP locks the voice but leaves the address label readable so the network can still handle it. It needs a separate way to hand out the key.

sections.title: Key Management for SRTP
sections.content:
Several schemes supply SRTP keys.

  • DTLS-SRTP: key exchange in the media plane between peers, with perfect forward secrecy and normally two round trips, or one with TLS resumption. Signaling carries certificate hashes to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. It is mandatory to support in WebRTC and growing among SIP endpoints.
  • MIKEY: several modes (pre-shared key, public key, Diffie-Hellman, HMAC-authenticated Diffie-Hellman, RSA-R, TICKET, IBAKE, SAKKE) for point-to-point, broadcast and group use.
  • Security descriptions: plaintext keys in SDP. Because signaling nodes can see them, their security properties are weak in most cases, yet they are the most commonly deployed solution for SIP endpoints.
  • EKT: lets group keys work with DTLS-SRTP through an additional key; the only known deployment is in some Cisco video conferencing products.
  • ZRTP: best-effort encryption independent of signaling, published as Informational rather than Standards Track.
sections.plainLanguage: Locking a box is only half the job; you also have to give the friend the key safely. Some ways whisper it directly, and some write it on a note that helpers could read.

sections.title: Other Mechanisms
sections.content:
The legacy confidentiality in RFC 3550 (DES or 3DES with keys in SDP) has extremely weak security and is not to be used. IPsec can protect RTP between network interfaces and suits infrastructure nodes with many sessions, but a VPN ending before the RTP endpoint leaves traffic exposed on the last stretch.

RTP over TLS over TCP gives point-to-point security, and is used by RTSP. DTLS can wrap complete RTP packets with no headers in the clear, which differs from DTLS-SRTP; the RFC sees no significant usage of DTLS for RTP. Media content security or DRM encrypts only the payload, letting middleboxes switch streams without reading content, but usually needs two layers of security and two key systems. ISMACryp is an example.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides SRTP there are tunnels, wrapped connections and locks that cover only the contents, each good for a different job.

sections.title: What to Weigh When Choosing
sections.content:
Application designers should consider the following.

  • Confidentiality: how long content must stay secret, leaks such as packet sizes with variable bitrate speech codecs, and who has access to the keys.
  • Integrity and source authentication: hop-by-hop or end-to-end, and who asserts it. Without a verifiable identifier, group keys can show only group membership.
  • Privacy: IP addresses can be hidden by a relay such as TURN, and RTCP CNAMEs in the form user@host allow tracking, so random ones per RFC 7022 are better.
  • Key management: automatic is preferred, and for SRTP it must prevent two-time pads from reuse of the same key and SSRC.
  • Tunnels and plaintext keys: end-to-end mechanisms are preferred over tunnels, and plaintext keys need trusted signaling.
  • Interoperability: it can conflict with security goals and supporting several mechanisms invites bid-down attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Before picking a lock, ask who must not look, who holds the key, and whether helpers in the middle can be trusted.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Five examples illustrate the choices. For SIP-established sessions, the IETF evaluated the options in 2009 and picked DTLS-SRTP, with the SIP signaling exchanging certificate fingerprints. Its main weakness is dependence on signaling that usually has only hop-by-hop protection.

WebRTC mandates SRTP keyed by DTLS-SRTP and can verify certificate hashes through an identity provider. IMS mostly uses end-to-access-edge security with security descriptions over trusted, encrypted SIP. 3GPP PSS uses ISMACryp with DRM, and the RFC notes it has no integrity check on RTP headers. RTSP 2.0 mandates SRTP keyed by MIKEY in RSA-R mode with TLS-protected signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: Chat apps in browsers, phone networks and video streaming each picked their own lock, and the guide shows why.
